title: Alert Fatigue
summary: Alert fatigue is the degradation of analyst attention and judgement caused by a detection pipeline that raises more alerts than a team can meaningfully examine. It is not simply a volume problem. Fatigue sets in when alerts are numerous and individually low-yield, so that the rational response becomes pattern matching on the alert title, batch-closing whole categories, and treating the queue as work to be cleared rather than as evidence to be assessed. The operational consequences are measurable: rising time to acknowledge the alerts that matter, missed true positives hidden inside noisy detections, analyst burnout and turnover, and a dangerous normalisation of anomalous activity. The root causes are structural. Rules built on a single event with no threshold, no entity context and no business weighting will fire on legitimate administrative behaviour. Log sources with poor parsing produce malformed fields that make every alert look identical. Duplicate detections from overlapping content raise the same activity several times. Suppressions are applied permanently instead of with an expiry, so detections quietly die and nobody notices the resulting blind spot. Because fatigue is a measurement and content-quality problem, the treatment is engineering rather than exhortation. Teams track per-rule alert volume against per-rule confirmed-true rate, retire or rewrite rules below a usefulness threshold, add allow-listing with mandatory expiry, enrich alerts with asset and identity context before an analyst ever sees them, and consolidate overlapping detections. Detection content then becomes a maintained product with owners, review dates and a documented reason to exist.
objectives: You will be able to explain how alert volume, low yield and duplicate content interact to produce analyst over-trust in titles and batch closures.
You will be able to measure per-rule alert volume against confirmed-true rate and use it to identify content that should be rewritten or retired.
You will be able to add entity context and thresholds to a noisy rule without destroying its ability to catch the behaviour it targets.
You will be able to design suppressions with mandatory expiry, ownership and a review condition rather than permanent exclusions.
You will be able to evaluate the operational cost of a detection before deploying it, including expected daily volume at current estate scale.
You will be able to argue a defensible case for retiring a detection while documenting the compensating control for the coverage it removes.
